cellular-respiration-s1.title: Peas in a respirometer
cellular-respiration-s1.text: A respirometer is a sealed vial with a thin, graduated glass tube. Each vial held a small pad soaked in potassium hydroxide (KOH), which absorbs CO₂, under a cotton plug, and was held in a water bath. As organisms in the vial take in O₂, the gas volume shrinks and a drop of colored water moves along the tube, showing the volume of gas used. Each vial held the same total volume of material: germinating peas, dry (dormant) peas plus glass beads, or glass beads alone. Values are means of 3 vials.

table.caption: Volume of gas taken up (mL) since time 0

cellular-respiration-s2.title: Oxygen use by isolated mitochondria
cellular-respiration-s2.text: Mitochondria isolated from liver were placed in a sealed chamber with pyruvate as fuel, and an electrode recorded the O₂ concentration. Additions: at 2 min, ADP and Pi; at 6 min, oligomycin, a drug that blocks the H⁺ channel of ATP synthase; at 10 min, DNP, a chemical that carries H⁺ across membranes; at 14 min, cyanide, which blocks the last protein of the electron transport chain.

cellular-respiration-s3.title: Yeast with and without oxygen
cellular-respiration-s3.text: Two flasks held equal amounts of yeast in glucose solution at 30 °C for one hour. One was bubbled with air; the other was sealed after the air was replaced with nitrogen gas, so it had no O₂. The table shows what the yeast used and made.

cellular-respiration-s4.title: Mice without the uncoupling protein
cellular-respiration-s4.text: Brown fat cells contain an uncoupling protein, UCP1, in their inner mitochondrial membrane. Researchers compared normal mice with mice that cannot make UCP1. Each mouse was moved from 22 °C to 4 °C for 6 hours. Mitochondria were then isolated from their brown fat and given fuel but no ADP, and their O₂ use and heat output were measured. Values are mean ± SD, 8 mice per group.

table.caption: Normal mice and mice lacking UCP1 after 6 hours at 4 °C
rows: O₂ use by brown-fat mitochondria (nmol/min per mg protein)
Heat output of brown-fat mitochondria (% of normal mean)

items.q: Correct the germinating peas at 25 °C using the beads-only vial at 25 °C. What is their average rate of O₂ use over the 20 minutes, in mL per minute? Give three decimal places.

why.correct: Corrected volume = 0.84 − 0.02 = 0.82 mL. Rate = 0.82 mL ÷ 20 min = 0.041 mL/min.

items.q: Why does each vial contain KOH?
options: It removes the CO₂ the peas release, so the change in gas volume shows O₂ taken up alone.
It supplies O₂ to the peas, so that they can keep respiring for the full 20 minutes.
It keeps the temperature inside each vial steady, so that the water bath does not warm the gas.
It kills bacteria on the peas, so that just the peas' own respiration is measured in the vial.

why.correct: Respiring peas take in O₂ and give out CO₂. If the CO₂ stayed as gas the two would nearly cancel; KOH absorbs the CO₂, so the shrinking volume measures O₂ used.
options: Removing CO₂ lets the volume change track O₂ uptake.
KOH absorbs CO₂; it does not produce O₂.
The water bath holds the temperature; KOH has a chemical job.
KOH is there to absorb CO₂; nothing in the setup is aimed at bacteria.

items.q: What is the purpose of the vials containing beads only?
options: They show volume changes not caused by respiration, such as shifts in temperature or pressure.
They show how much O₂ the glass beads themselves use, so that the beads can be subtracted from the dry-pea vial.
They give the peas in the other vials extra space, so that the peas do not run out of O₂.
They show the O₂ use of germinating peas at a lower rate, for comparison with the dry peas.

why.correct: Beads do not respire, so any movement in their tube comes from physical changes. Subtracting it corrects every vial at that temperature.
options: Beads-only vials are a control for physical changes in gas volume.
Glass beads are not alive and use no O₂; any reading is a physical change.
Each vial is separate; beads in one vial do nothing for peas in another.
The beads-only vials contain no peas at all.

items.q: Why do germinating peas use O₂ much faster than dry peas at the same temperature?
options: Germinating peas break down stored starch for ATP to grow; dry peas are dormant, with little metabolism.
Dry peas carry out photosynthesis inside the vial, which releases O₂ and hides their uptake of O₂.
Germinating peas are larger than dry peas, so more of their surface absorbs KOH and makes the drop move.
Dry peas lack mitochondria until they absorb water, so they are unable to carry out cellular respiration in the vial.

why.correct: A germinating seed is growing: it needs ATP, so it oxidizes its stored food quickly, using O₂. A dry seed's cells are nearly inactive.
options: Active growth needs ATP, which comes from respiration using O₂.
The vials are sealed and the peas are seeds; dry peas have no green leaves to photosynthesize, and the dry-pea vial shows a little uptake, not a release.
The vials hold the same total volume, and peas do not absorb KOH; the drop moves because O₂ is used.
Dry seeds do have mitochondria; their respiration is very slow, not absent (0.06 mL in 20 minutes).

items.q: Corrected O₂ use by germinating peas is 0.82 mL at 25 °C and 0.32 mL at 10 °C over 20 minutes. Which explanation and prediction are best supported?
options: Respiration's enzymes run slower at 10 °C, so at 30 °C the peas would likely use O₂ faster than at 25 °C.
Cold denatures the enzymes of respiration, so the peas at 10 °C would not recover if they were warmed again.
Peas at 10 °C need less ATP because they are colder, so they switch from respiration to photosynthesis.
The KOH absorbs CO₂ more slowly at 10 °C, so the cold vials show less gas taken up than was really used.

why.correct: Lower temperature means slower molecules and fewer energetic collisions, so enzyme-catalyzed respiration slows (to about 39%). Below the enzymes' optimum, warming speeds it up.
options: Enzyme rates rise with temperature up to their optimum, so 30 °C would likely be faster.
Cold slows enzymes but does not denature them; warming restores the rate.
Seeds in a dark sealed vial do not photosynthesize; they simply respire more slowly.
KOH works well at both temperatures; the beads-only correction already accounts for physical effects.

items.q: During which interval did the mitochondria use O₂ fastest?
options: 2-6 min
6-10 min

why.correct: From 10 to 14 min, O₂ fell from 140 to 20 nmol/mL: 30 per minute, the steepest slope.
options: After DNP, the slope is steepest: 120 nmol/mL in 4 minutes.
With ADP, O₂ fell 80 nmol/mL in 4 minutes (20 per minute), fast but not fastest.
After oligomycin, O₂ fell only 12 nmol/mL in 4 minutes.
After cyanide, O₂ stayed at 20: no use at all.

items.q: What was the rate of O₂ use between 2 and 6 minutes, in nmol/mL per minute? Give a whole number.

why.correct: Rate = (232 − 152) ÷ (6 − 2) = 80 ÷ 4 = 20 nmol/mL per minute.

items.q: After oligomycin blocks ATP synthase at 6 minutes, O₂ use falls sharply even though the electron transport chain itself is not blocked. Why?
options: H⁺ is no longer able to flow back through ATP synthase, so the gradient grows until the chain stalls.
Oligomycin also blocks the last protein of the chain, so O₂ is unable to accept electrons from it.
Without ATP synthase working, the matrix runs out of the O₂ that ATP synthase normally releases.
The ADP added at 2 minutes has been used up by then, and ADP is the molecule that the chain hands its electrons to.

why.correct: Pumping and H⁺ return are linked. With the return route blocked, H⁺ piles up in the intermembrane space until pumping becomes too hard, and electron flow to O₂ slows almost to a stop.
options: A too-steep gradient holds back the chain: respiration is tied to ATP synthesis.
The stem says oligomycin blocks ATP synthase; and adding DNP later restores fast O₂ use, so the chain still works.
ATP synthase makes ATP; it does not release O₂.
Electrons go to O₂, not to ADP; and the drop happens right when oligomycin is added.

items.q: DNP, added at 10 minutes, carries H⁺ across membranes. Which statement about the period from 10 to 14 minutes is best supported?
options: O₂ use is fast because H⁺ leaks back through DNP, so the chain runs freely, but the energy becomes heat, not ATP.
O₂ use is fast because DNP unblocks ATP synthase, so the mitochondria are now making more ATP than at any earlier time.
O₂ use is fast because DNP is itself broken down using O₂, and the mitochondria use it as a fuel.
O₂ use is fast because DNP is an electron carrier that delivers extra electrons from pyruvate to the chain.

why.correct: DNP is an uncoupler: it lets H⁺ back into the matrix without ATP synthase. The gradient stays low, so the chain pumps and uses O₂ at full speed, while ATP synthase stays blocked by oligomycin.
options: Uncoupling separates electron flow from ATP synthesis; the energy is released as heat.
Oligomycin is still present, so ATP synthase stays blocked; DNP gives H⁺ another way back.
DNP's effect is to move H⁺, and O₂ use stops at once when cyanide is added, showing the chain, not DNP breakdown, uses the O₂.
The stem says DNP carries H⁺, not electrons.

items.q: Why did O₂ use stop completely after cyanide was added, even though DNP was still present?
options: Cyanide stops electrons from reaching O₂, so no O₂ is reduced to water.
Cyanide blocks the H⁺ leak through DNP, so the gradient rebuilds and stops the pumping.
Cyanide uses up the O₂ left in the chamber by reacting with it directly.
Cyanide blocks ATP synthase, which had started making ATP again once DNP was added.

why.correct: Cyanide blocks the last protein of the chain, the one that hands electrons to O₂. With no electrons reaching O₂, O₂ use stops, whatever happens to the gradient.
options: Blocking the final transfer to O₂ stops O₂ use directly.
The stem says cyanide blocks the last protein of the chain, not DNP.
O₂ stays flat at 20 nmol/mL after cyanide, so nothing is using it up.
ATP synthase was already blocked by oligomycin; cyanide acts on the chain.

items.q: In the flask without O₂, how many molecules of CO₂ were released per molecule of glucose used? Give one decimal place.

why.correct: 3.80 mmol CO₂ ÷ 1.90 mmol glucose = 2.0, matching alcohol fermentation: glucose → 2 ethanol + 2 CO₂.

items.q: Assume about 30 ATP per glucose with O₂ and 2 per glucose without. Which claim do the data support?
options: With O₂ the yeast made about 3.5 times more ATP while using under a quarter as much glucose.
Without O₂ the yeast made more ATP, because they used over four times as much glucose.
The two flasks made about the same amount of ATP, because both released a similar amount of CO₂.
Without O₂ the yeast made no ATP, because ethanol and CO₂ were the sole products they made.

why.correct: With O₂: 0.45 × 30 ≈ 13.5 mmol ATP. Without: 1.90 × 2 = 3.8 mmol ATP. 13.5 ÷ 3.8 ≈ 3.5, while glucose use was 0.45 against 1.90.
options: Respiration with O₂ gets far more ATP from each glucose.
1.90 × 2 = 3.8 mmol is less than 0.45 × 30 ≈ 13.5 mmol.
CO₂ is not a measure of ATP; the two pathways release different CO₂ per ATP.
Glycolysis still makes 2 ATP per glucose during fermentation.

items.q: Why do yeast without O₂ turn pyruvate into ethanol instead of simply stopping after glycolysis?
options: Making ethanol passes NADH's electrons on, regenerating NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep running.
Making ethanol releases more ATP than glycolysis, which is the main energy source without O₂.
Ethanol is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain when no O₂ is available.
Ethanol is needed to build new yeast cells, so the yeast make it in large amounts whether O₂ is present or not.

why.correct: Glycolysis needs NAD⁺ to accept electrons. Without O₂, NADH cannot unload at the chain, so it gives its electrons to a molecule made from pyruvate, which becomes ethanol. The NAD⁺ released keeps glycolysis going.
options: Fermentation's job is to recycle NAD⁺, not to make extra ATP.
Fermentation makes no ATP beyond glycolysis's 2.
Fermentation does not use the electron transport chain at all.
The flask with O₂ made almost no ethanol (0.02 mmol), so ethanol is not made regardless.

items.q: In the flask with O₂, the yeast released 2.70 mmol CO₂ from 0.45 mmol glucose. What does this ratio show?
options: About 6 CO₂ per glucose: all six carbons were oxidized, as in aerobic respiration.
About 2 CO₂ per glucose, so the yeast fermented glucose to ethanol even when O₂ was present.
About 0.17 CO₂ per glucose, so most of the glucose's carbon was kept as ethanol.
About 6 CO₂ per glucose, which shows the CO₂ came from the O₂ that was bubbled into the flask.

why.correct: 2.70 ÷ 0.45 = 6.0: all six carbons of each glucose left as CO₂, the result of glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle.
options: Six CO₂ per glucose is complete oxidation of all six carbons.
The ratio is 6, not 2, and almost no ethanol was made.
This divides glucose by CO₂ instead of CO₂ by glucose.
The carbon in CO₂ comes from glucose; O₂ accepts electrons and becomes water.

items.q: Which claim is best supported by the data?
options: UCP1 is needed for brown fat to produce enough heat to keep a mouse warm in the cold.
UCP1 is needed for brown-fat mitochondria to make ATP, which the mice burn to stay warm.
Mice lacking UCP1 have no brown fat, so their mitochondria use less O₂ in each tissue of the body.
Mice lacking UCP1 keep their body temperature as well as normal mice by shivering instead.

why.correct: Without UCP1, brown-fat mitochondria made 28% of the normal heat, and the mice cooled to 31.0 °C against 36.4 °C; the error bars do not come close.
options: Lower heat output and lower body temperature both point to UCP1's role in heat production.
UCP1 lets H⁺ bypass ATP synthase, so it reduces ATP made per O₂; its job is heat.
Brown-fat mitochondria were isolated from both groups, so these mice do have brown fat; other tissues were not measured.
Their body temperature was 5.4 °C lower, so they did not keep it as well.

items.q: Normal brown-fat mitochondria used O₂ rapidly even with no ADP added. Which explanation fits?
options: H⁺ leaks back into the matrix through UCP1, so the gradient stays low and the chain keeps going.
UCP1 makes ATP from AMP instead of ADP, so the mitochondria do not need any ADP added to run.
UCP1 carries electrons straight to O₂, so the electron transport chain in brown fat is bypassed.
Brown-fat mitochondria store large amounts of ADP, so adding more ADP had no effect on their use of O₂.

why.correct: Without ADP, ATP synthase cannot run and the gradient would normally build and slow the chain. UCP1 gives H⁺ another way back, so the chain keeps running and its energy is released as heat.
options: An H⁺ leak frees the chain from waiting on ATP synthesis.
UCP1 is a channel for H⁺; it makes no ATP.
UCP1 moves H⁺, not electrons; the chain still passes electrons to O₂.
Mice lacking UCP1 used far less O₂ under the same conditions, which points to UCP1, not stored ADP.

items.q: Compared with muscle mitochondria, how much ATP would you expect normal brown-fat mitochondria to make for each O₂ molecule they use?
options: Less, because many H⁺ return through UCP1 instead of ATP synthase.
More, because they use O₂ faster, and faster O₂ use means more ATP.
The same, because each mitochondrion makes a fixed amount of ATP per O₂.
More, because their extra heat speeds up ATP synthase.

why.correct: Each H⁺ that leaks through UCP1 is an H⁺ that does not turn ATP synthase. More O₂ is used per ATP, and the difference is released as heat.
options: Uncoupling lowers ATP made per O₂ used.
Fast O₂ use here is driven by the leak, not by ATP synthesis.
The ratio depends on how much H⁺ goes through ATP synthase, which UCP1 reduces.
Heat comes from the leak; it does not make ATP synthase produce more ATP.

items.q: Why were the isolated brown-fat mitochondria given fuel but no ADP when their O₂ use was measured?
options: With ATP synthase idle, any O₂ use reflects H⁺ returning by another route, such as UCP1.
ADP would have reacted with the fuel and used it up before the mitochondria could take any in.
Without ADP the mitochondria make extra ATP, which makes the difference between the two groups larger.
ADP is toxic to isolated mitochondria from mice that lack UCP1, so it had to be left out of both groups.

why.correct: Without ADP, ATP synthase cannot make ATP, so H⁺ cannot return through it. Normally the gradient would then stall the chain. Fast O₂ use in that condition shows a leak; comparing the two groups ties the leak to UCP1.
options: Removing ADP takes ATP synthase out of the picture, isolating the leak.
ADP does not react with the fuel; it is a substrate of ATP synthase.
ATP synthase needs ADP; without it, no ATP is made.
Nothing suggests ADP is toxic; it is a normal substrate in every mitochondrion.

items.q: Where in a eukaryotic cell does the Krebs cycle take place?
options: In the mitochondrial matrix
In the cytosol
In the inner mitochondrial membrane
In the intermembrane space

why.correct: The Krebs cycle's enzymes are dissolved in the matrix, inside the inner membrane, as are those of pyruvate oxidation.
options: The matrix holds the Krebs cycle enzymes.
Glycolysis happens in the cytosol.
The electron transport chain and ATP synthase are in the inner membrane.
The intermembrane space is where H⁺ accumulates.

items.q: A rat is fed glucose in which every carbon atom is radioactive, and it breathes normal air. Where will most of the radioactive carbon appear first outside the body?
options: In the CO₂ the rat breathes out
In the water the rat breathes out
In the O₂ the rat breathes out
In the urea in the rat's urine

why.correct: The carbons of glucose leave as CO₂ in pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle, and the CO₂ is breathed out.
options: Glucose's carbons become CO₂, which is exhaled.
Water forms from O₂, electrons and H⁺; it contains no carbon.
O₂ contains no carbon, and the rat takes it in rather than giving it out.
Urea carries nitrogen from amino acids; glucose has no nitrogen.

items.q: In a human muscle cell, select the two stages that release CO₂.
options: Pyruvate oxidation
Krebs cycle
Glycolysis
Electron transport chain
Lactic acid fermentation

why.correct: Each pyruvate loses one carbon as CO₂ in pyruvate oxidation, and the Krebs cycle releases the remaining two per acetyl CoA: 6 CO₂ per glucose in all.
options: One CO₂ per pyruvate, 2 per glucose.
Two CO₂ per acetyl CoA, 4 per glucose.
Glycolysis splits a six-carbon sugar into two three-carbon pyruvates; no carbon is lost.
The chain moves electrons and H⁺; it releases no carbon.
Lactic acid fermentation turns pyruvate into lactate, keeping all three carbons; alcohol fermentation in yeast does release CO₂.

items.q: Select the statement that is true of fermentation in human muscle cells.
options: It regenerates NAD⁺ by passing electrons from NADH to pyruvate.
It makes about 30 ATP per glucose when O₂ runs low.
It uses the electron transport chain with lactate as the final electron acceptor.
It takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.
It releases CO₂ from each pyruvate.

why.correct: Muscle fermentation turns pyruvate into lactate using NADH's electrons, freeing NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue. It happens in the cytosol and makes no extra ATP.
options: Regenerating NAD⁺ is the whole point of fermentation.
Fermentation gives only glycolysis's 2 ATP per glucose.
Fermentation does not use the electron transport chain.
Fermentation happens in the cytosol, next to glycolysis.
Lactate keeps all three carbons of pyruvate; no CO₂ is released.

items.q: Cyanide is added to cultured human cells, blocking the last protein of the electron transport chain. Predict the change in each variable over the next few minutes.

variables.name: O₂ used by the cells
variables.why: Electrons can no longer be passed to O₂, so O₂ is not reduced to water.

variables.name: H⁺ concentration in the intermembrane space
variables.why: With electrons stuck, the chain stops pumping H⁺, while H⁺ keeps flowing back through ATP synthase, so the gradient runs down.

variables.name: ATP made by oxidative phosphorylation
variables.why: ATP synthase needs the H⁺ gradient, which is fading.

variables.name: Lactate made by the cells
variables.why: NADH can no longer unload at the chain, so cells turn to fermentation to regenerate NAD⁺ for glycolysis, making lactate.

variables.name: Number of mitochondria in each cell
variables.why: Cyanide blocks a protein; it does not destroy mitochondria or make new ones within minutes.

why.correct: Blocking the final transfer to O₂ stops the chain, the gradient and most ATP synthesis; cells fall back on glycolysis and fermentation.

items.q: A gram of fat yields more than twice as much ATP as a gram of glucose when oxidized. Which explanation is best?
options: Fatty acids have far more hydrogen and less oxygen per carbon, so they supply more electrons to the chain.
Fats are broken down by glycolysis twice, because each fat molecule contains two glucose units joined by an ester bond.
Fats are oxidized in the cytosol, where ATP synthase works faster than it does inside the mitochondria.
Fats skip the electron transport chain and make their ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation instead.

why.correct: Fatty acids are long chains of –CH₂– groups: highly reduced, with lots of electron-rich hydrogen. Cut into acetyl CoA, they load many NADH and FADH₂, which drive more oxidative phosphorylation.
options: More electrons per gram means more NADH and FADH₂, so more ATP.
Fats are made of glycerol and fatty acids, not glucose.
Fatty acids are broken down in the mitochondria, and ATP synthase sits in the inner membrane.
Most ATP from fat comes from the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.

items.q: Which comparison of chemiosmosis in chloroplasts and in mitochondria is correct?
options: Chloroplasts pump H⁺ into the thylakoid space and make ATP in the stroma; mitochondria pump into the intermembrane space and make ATP in the matrix.
In both, H⁺ is pumped into the same compartment where ATP is made, and then flows back out through ATP synthase.
In chloroplasts the electrons come from glucose; in mitochondria they come from splitting water.
In chloroplasts O₂ is the final electron acceptor; in mitochondria NADP⁺ is the final electron acceptor.

why.correct: Both pump H⁺ into a compartment separate from where ATP is made (thylakoid space, intermembrane space), and ATP synthase makes ATP as H⁺ flows back into the stroma or matrix.
options: The two systems mirror each other; the H⁺ store and the ATP-making side are on opposite sides of the membrane.
H⁺ is pumped away from the ATP-making side and flows back to it through ATP synthase.
This reverses the electron sources: water in chloroplasts, food molecules in mitochondria.
This reverses the acceptors: NADP⁺ in chloroplasts, O₂ in mitochondria.

items.q: In a cell that cannot ferment, removing O₂ soon stops glycolysis too, although glycolysis itself uses no O₂. Why?
options: With the chain stopped, NADH has nowhere to unload and NAD⁺ runs out, so glycolysis stalls.
Glycolysis needs the ATP made by the chain as its starting energy, and the chain makes no ATP when O₂ is missing.
Without O₂ the cytosol becomes too acidic for the enzymes of glycolysis, which denature within seconds.
Pyruvate turns into O₂ when O₂ is absent, and this O₂ blocks the first enzyme of glycolysis by feedback.

why.correct: Glycolysis needs a steady supply of NAD⁺. Without O₂ to accept electrons, NADH piles up and NAD⁺ is used up; with no fermentation to recycle it, glycolysis stops.
options: The NAD⁺ supply links glycolysis to O₂ indirectly.
Glycolysis does use 2 ATP to start, but it makes 4, so it does not depend on the chain for ATP.
Nothing suggests a fast pH crash; the immediate problem is the missing NAD⁺.
Pyruvate cannot turn into O₂; this is not a real reaction.
